pos: n. (the Premonstratensian abbey near Ravensburg, founded 1145, keeper of a famous relic of the Holy Blood)
etymology: German weiss, white, and Au, a water meadow; the white meadow.
biblical_def: Weissenau near Ravensburg in Upper Swabia was founded in 1145 by Gebizo of Ravensburg and settled from Rot an der Rot. Its fame through the Middle Ages rested on a relic of the Holy Blood, given in 1283, which drew pilgrims and processions and is still carried in a mounted procession at Ravensburg. The church was rebuilt in baroque between 1717 and 1724 by Franz Beer; the abbey was dissolved in 1802 and the buildings became an asylum and later a psychiatric hospital. This dictionary records Weissenau for the relic, because the thing it claimed to hold is the most precious thing in Scripture and the claim is exactly the problem. The blood of Christ is the price of redemption and is called precious, “But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot” (1Pe 1:19). It purges the conscience, “purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God” (Heb 9:14). Without its shedding there is no remission, “without shedding of blood is no remission” (Heb 9:22). And it makes peace, “having made peace through the blood of his cross” (Col 1:20) — a work complete and never resident in a phial.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a relic as the remains of a holy person preserved and venerated; blood as the fluid which circulates in the body; redemption as deliverance by payment of a price; a pilgrimage as a journey to a shrine; and veneration as the highest degree of respect.
webster_full: RELIC, n. That which remains; the remains of the body of a saint, or of any holy person, preserved and venerated.
BLOOD, n. The fluid which circulates through the arteries and veins of the human body and of other animals; also, in Scripture, life; and the atoning sacrifice.
REDEMPTION, n. Repurchase of captured goods or prisoners; deliverance from sin and the penalties of God's violated law, by the atonement of Christ.
PILGRIMAGE, n. A long journey, particularly a journey to some place deemed sacred and venerable, in order to pay devotion to the relics of some deceased saint.
VENERATION, n. The highest degree of respect and reverence; respect mingled with some degree of awe.
scriptures: But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot:
Heb 9:14
How much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?
Heb 9:22
And almost all things are by the law purged with blood; and without shedding of blood is no remission.
Col 1:20
And, having made peace through the blood of his cross, by him to reconcile all things unto himself; by him, I say, whether they be things in earth, or things in heaven.
corruption_summary: Swabian Premonstratensian abbey of 1145: its relic of the Holy Blood drew pilgrims for five centuries, and the work that blood did was already finished.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture speaks of the blood of Christ with the highest possible value and never as a substance to be possessed. It is the ransom price, “But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish” (1Pe 1:19); it reaches the conscience, which no object can, “purge your conscience from dead works” (Heb 9:14); and it is the ground of peace with God, “having made peace through the blood of his cross” (Col 1:20).

The live error is the one the relic embodies: the attempt to make a finished work locally available in a thing. The letter to the Hebrews is written against precisely this instinct, insisting on one offering, once, in heaven rather than on an altar anyone can visit, and it draws the conclusion flatly, “without shedding of blood is no remission” (Heb 9:22), which places the whole weight on an event rather than on an object. The principle to recover is that what the pilgrims wanted was real and is already theirs without the journey.

pos: n. (the Swabian Premonstratensian abbey of 1125, since 1884 a great institution for the disabled)
etymology: From German Ur, aurochs or origin, and Berg, a hill.
biblical_def: Ursberg in Bavarian Swabia was founded in 1125 and became Premonstratensian in 1143; its abbot Burchard wrote a chronicle that remains a source for the twelfth century. The abbey was dissolved in 1802, and in 1884 the buildings were bought for a foundation caring for people with disabilities, which the Sisters of St Joseph have run ever since. It is now one of the largest such institutions in Germany, with thousands of residents, workshops and schools, and it has continued through a period in which the German state was murdering exactly these people. This dictionary records Ursberg for that work, because Scripture's valuation of the weak is explicit and inverts the natural one. The members that seem feeblest are called necessary, “those members of the body, which seem to be more feeble, are necessary” (1Co 12:22), and the less honourable are given more honour on purpose, “upon these we bestow more abundant honour” (1Co 12:23). The guest list Christ prescribes is of those who cannot repay, “call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind” (Luk 14:13), and he puts himself among them, “Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me” (Mat 25:40).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines infirmity as an unsound state of the body; feeble as weak or destitute of strength; lame as crippled or disabled in a limb; to succour as to help one in distress; and compassion as a suffering with another.
webster_full: INFIRMITY, n. An unsound or unhealthy state of the body; weakness; feebleness; also, a failing; a foible.
FEEBLE, adj. Weak; destitute of much physical strength; as feeble hands; also, wanting in force or vigor.
LAME, adj. Crippled or disabled in a limb, or otherwise injured so as to be unsound and impaired in strength.
SUCCOR, v.t. To run to, or run to support; hence, to help or relieve when in difficulty, want or distress; to assist and deliver from suffering.
COMPASSION, n. A suffering with another; painful sympathy; a sensation of sorrow excited by the distress or misfortunes of another.
scriptures: Nay, much more those members of the body, which seem to be more feeble, are necessary:
And those members of the body, which we think to be less honourable, upon these we bestow more abundant honour; and our uncomely parts have more abundant comeliness.
But when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind:
And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.
corruption_summary: Swabian abbey of 1125, since 1884 a foundation for the disabled: it kept its residents through a regime that was killing them.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Paul's, and it is an argument rather than a sentiment. He does not say the weak should be tolerated; he says the seemingly feeble parts are necessary to the body, “those members of the body, which seem to be more feeble, are necessary” (1Co 12:22), and that honour is deliberately redistributed toward them, “upon these we bestow more abundant honour” (1Co 12:23). A church arranged on any other principle has stopped being a body.

The second thing is the test Christ supplies, which is whether a man invites people who cannot return the favour, “call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind” (Luk 14:13). He then identifies himself with the recipients in a way that removes any possibility of condescension, “ye have done it unto me” (Mat 25:40). Ursberg went on doing this through the years when the state had declared such lives worthless, which is what the doctrine looks like when it costs something.

pos: n. (the Bohemian Premonstratensian abbey of 1193, founded by Hroznata, who died in prison refusing ransom)
etymology: Czech teplá, warm, from the river of that name.
biblical_def: Teplá in western Bohemia was founded in 1193 by Hroznata, a Bohemian nobleman who had taken the cross, was released from his vow by the pope on condition that he found a monastery, and who afterwards entered the house himself as a canon. In 1217 he was seized by robber knights who demanded a ransom; he forbade the abbey to pay it, and died of hunger and cold in their prison. The abbey's library grew to around a hundred thousand volumes and survives. This dictionary records Teplá for Hroznata's refusal, and for the way Scripture handles prisoners. The church is commanded to remember those in bonds as though it shared the chains, “Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them” (Heb 13:3). Christ counts a visit to a prisoner as made to himself, “I was in prison, and ye came unto me” (Mat 25:36). A chained apostle observes that the chain does not reach the message, “but the word of God is not bound” (2Ti 2:9), and two men in a Philippian jail show what that looks like, “Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God” (Act 16:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a ransom as the money paid for the redemption of a prisoner; bonds as chains or imprisonment; a captive as one taken by an enemy; to redeem as to purchase back; and martyrdom as the death of a martyr.
webster_full: RANSOM, n. The money or price paid for the redemption of a prisoner or slave, or for goods captured by an enemy; release from captivity by payment.
BONDS, n. plu. Chains; fetters; imprisonment; captivity; also, obligations imposing a moral duty.
CAPTIVE, n. A prisoner taken by force or stratagem in war, by an enemy; one kept in bondage.
REDEEM, v.t. To purchase back; to ransom; to liberate or rescue from captivity or bondage, or from any obligation or liability.
MARTYRDOM, n. The death of a martyr; the suffering of death on account of adherence to the Christian faith, or to any article of it.
scriptures: Heb 13:3
Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them; and them which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body.
Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me.
Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound.
And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them.
corruption_summary: Bohemian abbey of 1193: its founder entered it as a canon and died in a robber's prison after forbidding the house to ransom him.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the command about prisoners, which asks for imagination rather than charity. Hebrews does not say to pity them but to remember them as if the chains were on your own wrists, “Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them” (Heb 13:3), and Christ makes the visit itself a service rendered to him, “I was in prison, and ye came unto me” (Mat 25:36).

Hroznata's refusal is harder to read, and the dictionary does not commend self-destruction. He judged that paying would fund more kidnapping and beggar the house, and he bore the consequence himself rather than imposing it. What Scripture does say about such a position is that the imprisonment never silences the thing that matters, “Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound” (2Ti 2:9), and that the behaviour of prisoners can be remarkable, “And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them” (Act 16:25).

pos: n. (the Bohemian Premonstratensian abbey of 1139, used as an internment camp for clergy from 1950)
etymology: From a Czech personal name Žela, with the possessive ending.
biblical_def: Želiv in the Bohemian-Moravian highlands was founded in 1139 for Benedictines and given to the Premonstratensians in 1149. Its church was rebuilt by Jan Blažej Santini-Aichel in a distinctive baroque Gothic between 1714 and 1720. In 1950 the Czechoslovak communist government suppressed the religious houses, and Želiv was turned into an internment camp through which some four hundred and sixty priests and religious passed, held without trial, some for years. It was returned to the Premonstratensians in 1991 and is a working abbey again. This dictionary records Želiv because an abbey converted into a prison for clergy is the clearest possible case of what Scripture tells the church to expect and how to bear it. Persecution is promised rather than threatened, “all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution” (2Ti 3:12). The response prescribed is not retaliation, “Love your enemies, bless them that curse you” (Mat 5:44). The sufferers are called blessed, “Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake” (Mat 5:10), and the assurance given is that nothing finally separates them, “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?” (Rom 8:35).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines persecution as the infliction of pain for adherence to a religion; to suppress as to put down by force; an internment as a confinement within limits; tyranny as arbitrary or despotic exercise of power; and constancy as firmness of mind.
webster_full: PERSECUTION, n. The act or practice of persecuting; the infliction of pain, punishment or death upon others unjustly, particularly for adhering to a religious creed.
SUPPRESS, v.t. To overpower and crush; to subdue; to destroy; to put an end to; as, to suppress a rebellion or an institution.
CONFINEMENT, n. Restraint within limits; imprisonment; any restraint of liberty by force or other obstacle.
TYRANNY, n. Arbitrary or despotic exercise of power; the exercise of power over subjects and others with a rigor not authorized by law or justice.
CONSTANCY, n. Firmness of mind; stability; steadiness; fixedness; particularly, firmness in adhering to a cause or to principles.
scriptures: Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution.
Mat 5:44
But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you;
Mat 5:10
Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
Rom 8:35
Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?
corruption_summary: Bohemian Premonstratensian abbey of 1139: a communist internment camp for some four hundred and sixty clergy, and a working abbey again since 1991.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture treats persecution as normal rather than exceptional, and says so in a sentence with no exemptions in it, “Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution” (2Ti 3:12). A church that regards a quiet century as the baseline will be disoriented by an ordinary one.

The second thing is the prescribed response, which is the hardest command in the Sermon on the Mount and was given to people under occupation, “Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you” (Mat 5:44). The sufferers are not pitied but congratulated, “for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Mat 5:10), and Paul runs through every instrument a state has and concludes that none of them reaches the thing that matters, “shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?” (Rom 8:35). Forty-one years later the canons came back.

pos: n. (the Premonstratensian abbey above Prague, founded 1143, guarding the approach to the castle)
etymology: From Czech strahovat, to watch over or guard; the watch post.
biblical_def: Strahov stands on the hill above Prague Castle and was founded in 1143 by Bishop Jindřich Zdík and Duke Vladislav II, the first Premonstratensian house in Bohemia. Its name is generally explained from the Czech for keeping watch, because the site guarded the western approach to the castle. The abbey survived Hussite wars, Swedish sack, Josephine reform and communist suppression, and it holds two of the most photographed rooms in Europe, the Theological Hall of 1679 and the Philosophical Hall of 1794. This dictionary records Strahov for its name, because the watchman is one of Scripture's most demanding offices. The sentry who sees danger and says nothing is charged with the blood of the people, “if the watchman see the sword come, and blow not the trumpet” (Eze 33:6). The office is given by appointment, not ambition, “Son of man, I have made thee a watchman unto the house of Israel” (Eze 3:17). The prophet takes his post and waits for an answer, “I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower” (Hab 2:1), and the question put to a watchman is always the same, “Watchman, what of the night?” (Isa 21:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a watchman as one set to guard; to watch as to be awake and vigilant; a sentinel as a soldier set to guard; vigilance as forbearance of sleep and watchfulness; and an alarm as a sound giving notice of danger.
webster_full: WATCHMAN, n. A sentinel; a guard; one set to watch in the night; one who guards a city or other place from danger.
WATCH, v.i. To be awake; to be or continue without sleep; to look with attention or steadiness; to be vigilant.
SENTINEL, n. In military affairs, a soldier set to watch or guard an army, camp or other place from surprise.
VIGILANCE, n. Forbearance of sleep; a state of being awake; watchfulness; circumspection; attention of the mind in discovering danger.
ALARM, n. Any sound, outcry or information intended to give notice of approaching danger; a summons to arms.
scriptures: Eze 33:6

But if the watchman see the sword come, and blow not the trumpet, and the people be not warned; if the sword come, and take any person from among them, he is taken away in his iniquity; but his blood will I require at the watchman's hand.
Eze 3:17
Son of man, I have made thee a watchman unto the house of Israel: therefore hear the word at my mouth, and give them warning from me.
Hab 2:1
I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower, and will watch to see what he will say unto me, and what I shall answer when I am reproved.
The burden of Dumah. He calleth to me out of Seir, Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?
corruption_summary: Premonstratensian abbey above Prague, 1143, named for keeping watch: it survived Hussites, Swedes, Josephine reform and communism, and keeps two great library halls.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the severity of the watchman's charge. Ezekiel is told that a sentry who sees the sword and stays silent is answerable for the deaths, “if the watchman see the sword come, and blow not the trumpet, and the people be not warned” (Eze 33:6). That is a frightening standard for any man who preaches, and it is given by appointment rather than taken up by preference, “Son of man, I have made thee a watchman unto the house of Israel” (Eze 3:17).

The second thing is the posture. Habakkuk does not pace; he takes a position and waits for God to answer his complaint, “I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower, and will watch to see what he will say unto me” (Hab 2:1). And Isaiah records the question that is always put to a watchman, with its odd, unsatisfying reply, “Watchman, what of the night?” (Isa 21:11). A house on a hill above a capital, under four successive regimes, had the name for a reason.

pos: n. (the Premonstratensian abbey on the upper Danube, whose white baroque church was built by the Vorarlberg masons)
etymology: German ober, upper, with Marchtal, the valley on the march or border.
biblical_def: Obermarchtal stands above the upper Danube in Württemberg. A house existed there from the ninth century; it was given to the Premonstratensians in 1171 and remained theirs until 1803. Between 1686 and 1701 the abbey rebuilt its church to a design by Michael Thumb and his brothers, the first great work of the Vorarlberg school of masons, and the interior is famous for being almost entirely white: white stucco, white walls, and light. After centuries of gilding this was a deliberate severity. This dictionary records Obermarchtal for that whiteness, because Scripture uses the colour for one thing consistently and it is not innocence but cleansing. The offer is made in the boldest possible terms, “though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow” (Isa 1:18). David asks for it as a washing, “wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” (Psa 51:7). The robes of the redeemed are white because of where they were washed, “have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev 7:14), and the linen granted to the bride is explained, “for the fine linen is the righteousness of saints” (Rev 19:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines white as being of the colour of pure snow; to cleanse as to free from filth; scarlet as a bright red colour; linen as cloth made of flax; and purity as freedom from foreign admixture or moral defilement.
webster_full: WHITE, adj. Being in the color of pure snow; snowy; not dark; pure; clean; free from spot; unblemished.
CLEANSE, v.t. To purify; to make clean; to free from filth; to purify from guilt; to free from a foul or infectious disease.
SCARLET, n. A beautiful bright red color, brighter than crimson; also, cloth of a scarlet color.
LINEN, n. Cloth made of flax or hemp; also, an under garment made of linen.
PURITY, n. Freedom from foreign admixture or heterogeneous matter; freedom from guilt or the defilement of sin; innocence.
scriptures: Isa 1:18
Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.
Psa 51:7
Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.
Rev 7:14
And I said unto him, Sir, thou knowest. And he said to me, These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.
Rev 19:8
And to her was granted that she should be arrayed in fine linen, clean and white: for the fine linen is the righteousness of saints.
corruption_summary: Premonstratensian abbey on the upper Danube: an all-white baroque interior by the Vorarlberg masons, and a colour Scripture uses for cleansing rather than innocence.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is what white actually signifies in Scripture. It is almost never the colour of people who have not sinned; it is the colour of people who have been washed, and Isaiah makes the offer in terms deliberately chosen to be hard to believe, “though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow” (Isa 1:18). David asks for the same thing after the worst year of his life, “wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” (Psa 51:7).

The second thing is where the washing happens, which is the one detail that keeps the image from becoming moralism. The robes in Revelation are not white because their wearers kept them clean, and the explanation is startling, “and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev 7:14). The linen is then identified, so that nobody mistakes the garment for the wearer's own achievement, “for the fine linen is the righteousness of saints” (Rev 19:8). A white church is a better sermon than a gilded one.

usage: “though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow” (Isa 1:18) — an offer framed to be hard to believe.
“and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev 7:14) — the detail that forbids moralism.
“for the fine linen is the righteousness of saints” (Rev 19:8) — the garment identified.

pos: n. (the Upper Palatinate Premonstratensian abbey of 1145, resettled in 1921)
etymology: From an Old High German personal name with hart, a wood or forest.
biblical_def: Speinshart in the Upper Palatinate was founded in 1145 by Adelvolk of Reifenberg and his wife Richinza and given to the Premonstratensians. It was ruined in the Thirty Years War, rebuilt from 1691, and its church finished in 1706 with stucco by the Carlone family of Italian artists whose illusionistic work makes a flat ceiling appear to open into sky. The abbey was dissolved in 1803 and resettled by Norbertines in 1921; it is a working house today with a school. This dictionary records Speinshart for that painted ceiling, because illusion is a subject Scripture addresses more often than beauty. The appearance of a thing is explicitly not the measure, “man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart” (1Sa 16:7). Judging by looks is forbidden, “Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment” (Joh 7:24). The adversary himself works by appearance, “Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light” (2Co 11:14), and the things that are actually permanent are the ones that cannot be seen, “the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal” (2Co 4:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines appearance as the thing seen or external show; illusion as deceptive appearance; stucco as a fine plaster for walls; to counterfeit as to imitate with a view to deceive; and sincerity as freedom from hypocrisy.
webster_full: APPEARANCE, n. The act of coming into sight; the thing seen; a phenomenon; semblance; external show; outside; as, the appearance of virtue.
ILLUSION, n. Deceptive appearance; false show, by which a person is or may be deceived, or his expectations disappointed; mockery.
STUCCO, n. A fine plaster, composed of lime, chalk and pulverized marble, used for the internal decoration of walls and ceilings.
COUNTERFEIT, v.t. To forge; to copy or imitate, without authority or right, and with a view to deceive or defraud, by passing the copy for original.
SINCERITY, n. Honesty of mind or intention; freedom from simulation or hypocrisy; purity; freedom from any foreign admixture.
scriptures: But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
Joh 7:24
Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.
And no marvel; for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light.
While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal.
corruption_summary: Upper Palatinate abbey of 1145, resettled 1921: a Carlone ceiling that appears to open into sky, over a house that was twice a ruin.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture is consistently unimpressed by surfaces. Samuel is corrected at the moment he is most confident, and the reason given has become proverbial, “for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart” (1Sa 16:7). The Lord makes the same point as a command about how to judge, “Judge not according to the appearance” (Joh 7:24).

The live corruption is the assumption that the impressive and the true travel together. Paul warns that the enemy's characteristic method is a convincing appearance rather than an obvious horror, “Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light” (2Co 11:14), and he inverts the ordinary ranking of the visible and the invisible in a sentence worth memorising, “the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal” (2Co 4:18). A ceiling painted to look like heaven is lovely and is plaster.

Greek opsis (G3799) — the look of a thing; “Judge not according to the appearance”, John 7:24.
Greek metaschematizo (G3345) — to change one's outward form; “Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light”, 2 Corinthians 11:14.
Greek proskairos (G4340) — temporary, for a season; “the things which are seen are temporal”, 2 Corinthians 4:18.

“Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light” (2Co 11:14) — the method is a convincing surface.
“the things which are not seen are eternal” (2Co 4:18) — the ranking inverted.

pos: n. (the Premonstratensian abbey in the Bavarian Forest, founded 1140, refounded 1923 as a youth house)
etymology: German Wind, wind, and Berg, a hill; the windy hill.
biblical_def: Windberg in the Bavarian Forest was founded about 1140 by Count Albert I of Bogen and given to the Premonstratensians. Its Romanesque church of 1167 survives with a celebrated carved portal, under a baroque remodelling of the eighteenth century. The abbey was dissolved in 1803 and resettled by Norbertines from Berne in the Netherlands in 1923, since when its principal work has been a youth education house that receives thousands of young people a year. This dictionary records Windberg for that work, because the instruction of the young is one of the duties Scripture states most plainly and most often. The charge is to the household first, “ye shall teach them your children, speaking of them when thou sittest in thine house” (Deu 11:19). The training has a direction and a long horizon, “Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it” (Pro 22:6). Fathers are told how not to do it, “provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord” (Eph 6:4), and Timothy's case shows the method's power, “from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures” (2Ti 3:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a child as a son or daughter; to train as to discipline for a purpose; nurture as that which nourishes and educates; admonition as gentle reproof; and instruction as the act of teaching.
webster_full: CHILD, n. A son or a daughter; a male or female descendant in the first degree; the immediate progeny of parents.
TRAIN, v.t. To draw along; to educate; to teach; to form by instruction or practice; to bring up and discipline.
NURTURE, n. That which nourishes; food; diet; also, instruction; education; the discipline which forms manners and character.
ADMONITION, n. Gentle reproof; counseling against a fault; instruction in duties; caution; direction.
INSTRUCTION, n. The act of teaching or informing the understanding in that of which it was before ignorant; information.
scriptures: And ye shall teach them your children, speaking of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
Pro 22:6
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
Eph 6:4
And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.
And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: Bavarian Forest abbey of 1140, refounded 1923: its main work is a youth house that receives thousands of young people a year.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that teaching the young is assigned to the household and only then to anyone else. Moses puts it in the ordinary hours of a day rather than in a timetable, “speaking of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way” (Deu 11:19), and Solomon gives the horizon on which the work is measured, which is decades long, “and when he is old, he will not depart from it” (Pro 22:6).

The live corruption runs in two directions at once: parents who outsource the whole business to an institution, and institutions that treat the young as a market rather than a charge. Paul addresses fathers with a warning about manner before method, “And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath” (Eph 6:4), and sets the content as nurture and admonition rather than entertainment. Timothy knew the Scriptures from infancy, and Paul names that as the reason he could stand, “which are able to make thee wise unto salvation” (2Ti 3:15).

“and when he is old, he will not depart from it” (Pro 22:6) — a horizon measured in decades.
“provoke not your children to wrath” (Eph 6:4) — manner before method.

pos: n. (the Premonstratensian abbey in the Bohemian Forest of Upper Austria, founded 1218)
etymology: From German Schlag, a felling or clearing in a wood.
biblical_def: Schlägl in the Mühlviertel of Upper Austria, close against the Bohemian border, was founded in 1202 for Cistercians, failed, and was refounded for the Premonstratensians in 1218. It has been a working abbey for eight centuries with only brief interruption, including the Nazi years when the canons were expelled. Its wealth has always been timber: the abbey still manages several thousand hectares of forest in the Mühlviertel, along with a brewery and a school. This dictionary records Schlägl for the forest, because trees are one of Scripture's steadiest figures for a settled life. The blessed man is a tree by water that does not fail in drought, “his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper” (Psa 1:3). The righteous grow like a cedar, “he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon” (Psa 92:12), and still bear in age, “They shall still bring forth fruit in old age” (Psa 92:14). The name God gives the restored is arboreal, “that they might be called trees of righteousness, the planting of the LORD” (Isa 61:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a forest as an extensive wood; timber as wood suitable for building; a cedar as a large evergreen tree; to flourish as to thrive or grow luxuriantly; and to plant as to set in the ground for growth.
webster_full: FOREST, n. An extensive wood, or a large tract of land covered with trees; a wood of great extent.
TIMBER, n. That sort of wood which is proper for buildings or for tools, utensils, furniture, carriages, fences, ships and the like.
CEDAR, n. The name of several species of trees, remarkable for durability and fragrance; the cedar of Lebanon is a large evergreen.
FLOURISH, v.i. To thrive; to grow luxuriantly; to increase and enlarge, as a healthy growing plant; to be prosperous.
PLANT, v.t. To set in the ground for growth; to settle; to fix the first inhabitants; to introduce and establish.
scriptures: Psa 1:3
And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper.
The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree: he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon.
They shall still bring forth fruit in old age; they shall be fat and flourishing;
Isa 61:3

To appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness; that they might be called trees of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that he might be glorified.
corruption_summary: Upper Austrian Premonstratensian abbey of 1218: eight centuries of continuous life, and thousands of hectares of forest still in its care.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the slowness of the figure. A tree is not a crop; it is measured in generations, and the psalm's promise concerns endurance under conditions that kill other plants, “his leaf also shall not wither” (Psa 1:3). A house that has managed the same woods for eight hundred years understands the timescale better than most institutions do.

The second thing is fruit in old age, which Scripture insists on against every assumption that usefulness has a term. The righteous are said to grow like a cedar, “he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon” (Psa 92:12), and the promise is explicit about the late years, “They shall still bring forth fruit in old age; they shall be fat and flourishing” (Psa 92:14). The title given to the restored is a planting rather than a rescue, “the planting of the LORD, that he might be glorified” (Isa 61:3).

pos: n. (the abbey on the Leie near Ghent, Premonstratensian from 1136, now a Jesuit retreat house)
etymology: From Old Dutch Thrudinga, the settlement of Thrud's people.
biblical_def: Drongen on the Leie just west of Ghent was an ancient foundation attached to the Premonstratensians in 1136 and dissolved at the French Revolution. The buildings passed to the Jesuits in 1837, who rebuilt them and have used the place ever since chiefly as a house of retreat, where people come for a week of silence. The eighteenth-century tower stands above a bend in the river. This dictionary records Drongen for that use, because the deliberate withdrawal of busy people for a short time is a practice the Lord himself prescribed to men who were too busy to eat. The instruction is given to workers, not to contemplatives, “Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while” (Mar 6:31). The reason is stated and is startlingly ordinary, “for there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat” (Mar 6:31). Rest is promised as a gift from a person, “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Mat 11:28), and promised again as something still outstanding, “There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God” (Heb 4:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a retreat as a place of retirement or security; rest as cessation of motion or labour; leisure as freedom from occupation; solitude as a lonely life; and refreshment as new strength after fatigue.
webster_full: RETREAT, n. The act of retiring; a place of retirement or privacy; a place of safety or security; retirement for religious exercises.
REST, n. Cessation of motion or action of any kind, and applicable to any body or being; quiet; repose; sleep.
LEISURE, n. Freedom from occupation or business; vacant time; time free from employment.
SOLITUDE, n. Loneliness; a state of being alone; a lonely life; also, a lonely place; a desert.
REFRESHMENT, n. The act of refreshing; new strength or vigor; relief after fatigue; that which gives fresh strength.
scriptures: Mar 6:31
And he said unto them, Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while: for there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat.
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
Heb 4:9
There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God.
And he said, My presence shall go with thee, and I will give thee rest.
corruption_summary: Abbey on the Leie near Ghent, Premonstratensian from 1136: a Jesuit house of retreat since 1837, where people come for a week of silence.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is who the instruction was given to. The apostles had just returned from preaching and healing, and the Lord sent them away to rest with a reason that any overworked person recognises, “for there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat” (Mar 6:31). Withdrawal here is not an alternative vocation but a repair of one.

The second thing is that rest in Scripture is finally a person and a promise rather than a practice. The invitation is addressed to the exhausted and the burdened, and what is offered is given rather than achieved, “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Mat 11:28). God's word to Moses ties the rest to his own presence, “My presence shall go with thee, and I will give thee rest” (Exo 33:14), and Hebrews insists that the real thing is still ahead, “There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God” (Heb 4:9). A week of silence is a foretaste, not the article.
roots_summary: Greek anapauo (G373), to rest; Greek eukaireo (G2119), to have leisure; Greek phortizo (G5412), to load; Hebrew nuach (H5117), to give rest; Greek sabbatismos (G4520), a sabbath rest.
roots_lines: Greek anapauo (G373) — to rest, to be refreshed; “Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while”, Mark 6:31.
Greek eukaireo (G2119) — to have leisure, which they lacked; “they had no leisure so much as to eat”, Mark 6:31.
Greek phortizo (G5412) — to be loaded, heavy laden; “all ye that labour and are heavy laden”, Matthew 11:28.
Hebrew nuach (H5117) — to settle, to give rest; “and I will give thee rest”, Exodus 33:14.
Greek sabbatismos (G4520) — a sabbath keeping, still ahead; “There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God”, Hebrews 4:9.
usage: “Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while” (Mar 6:31) — said to workers, not to contemplatives.
“I will give you rest” (Mat 11:28) — given, not achieved.
“There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God” (Heb 4:9) — the article, of which a week is a taste.
